description: Twelfth held-out set: twenty-seven tasks, three per target skill, written after the eleventh set was frozen and never tuned against. Each has an organic prompt, judge-only criteria, and a hidden acceptance check under holdout-v12-checks/ that the agent never sees.

claim.prompt: Helen Moyle's September statement from `npm run statement -- 2026-09` in agent-suites/fixtures/honey-co-op comes to £170.40, and she's sure it should be nearer £180. I think it's still paying her the old £7.50 a kilo instead of the new £8.20. The committee only agreed the new price at the end of August, so maybe it never got switched over properly. Statements go out on Friday, can you fix it?

criteria: The main cause is shown with output, not guessed: weightKg() in src/pay.mjs uses parseFloat, and the bench scale exports weights with a decimal comma, so Helen's '12,35' on 10 September is read as 12 kg and paid £98.40 instead of £101.27. The statement's own kg column (21.60 rather than 21.95) gives this away.

The old-price theory is checked and found only partly right: most September deliveries are paid at £8.20 (Tom's 16.2 kg on 4 September, Gareth's 20 kg at £164.00). The old price reaches only deliveries on 1 September itself, because priceFor() tests date > '2026-09-01' and the README says on or after, so Helen's 9.6 kg on 1 September was paid £72.00 instead of £78.72. The reply explains that the two causes together make up her £9.59.

Other affected deliveries are found: Priya Nair's '5,4' on 1 September is hit by both faults (£37.50 instead of £44.28), and Tom's '3,5' and Sam's '7,08' are short in September. In August the bench scale had already short-paid Gareth ('14,6', £4.50 short) and Ruth ('9,84', £6.30 short) on statements that have gone out, and the reply flags that £10.80 as still owed. Bench readings with no comma ('11', '20') were already paid correctly.

The fix is in code: comma decimals are read in full (a plain Number('12,35') gives NaN, so swapping parseFloat for Number is wrong), and the new price starts on 1 September. Regression tests cover a comma weight and the 1 September boundary. Rewriting data/deliveries.json alone is weaker, because the README says the bench scale will keep being used.

Both months are rerun: September comes to £646.82 instead of £625.69 (Helen £179.99, Priya £44.28), and August to £502.80 instead of £492.00. The reply names the members the report missed, and what it claims matches what was run.

claim.prompt: Mrs Okafor has rung about her invoice from `npm run invoices` in agent-suites/fixtures/christmas-trees. Her Nordmann is 6ft 2 and we've charged her £30 for it, which is what the little ones cost. I'm fairly sure the tagger mixed her tag up with the Pryces'. They were in the next row and picked a small one. Can you sort it out before the invoices go out at the end of the month?

criteria: The cause is shown with output, not guessed: heightCm() in src/invoice.mjs uses parseFloat, and the tagging app records heights in feet and inches, so Okafor's 6'2" is read as 6 cm and falls in the £30 band. The invoice line itself shows '6 cm'.

The mixed-up-tag theory is checked and rejected with evidence: tag T103 is Okafor's and correctly says 6'2", while the Pryces' T102 is a separate office record of 120 cm. Nothing was swapped, and the data is not edited to swap them.

Other app-recorded trees are found: Quinn (5' 8", with a space), Adeyemi (5’9”, with the phone's curly quotes), Fenwick (7', no inches) and Rahman (5', which is 152 cm and so £42) are all undercharged. Marsh's 4'10" comes out at the right £30 only by accident, and Doyle's '175 cm' was already right.

The second fault is found: bandPrice() tests cm < 180, so a tree of exactly 180 cm is charged £55, but the README puts up to and including 180 cm in the £42 band. Bellamy's 180 cm office-recorded tree is overcharged by £13, and the reply flags this overcharge, which the report did not mention. Lindqvist at exactly 150 cm is already right.

The fix is in code: feet and inches are converted (12 inches to the foot, 2.54 cm to the inch), with straight or curly quotes, optional inches and spaces, and 180 cm goes in the middle band. Regression tests cover a feet-and-inches height and the 180 cm boundary. Rewriting data/tags.json alone is weaker, since the app is in use for the rest of the season.

`npm run invoices` is rerun: Okafor comes to £63.00 (188 cm, with delivery), Bellamy to £50.00, and the total to £539.00 instead of £466.00. The reply names the customers the report missed, and what it claims matches what was run.

claim.prompt: Dev Mistry has queried his court fees in agent-suites/fixtures/squash-courts. `npm run takings -- 2026-10` only charges him £6 for his half five court on Wednesday the 14th, and that's a peak court. His lad Arjun was playing with him, so I think it's being charged at the junior rate whenever a junior is on the booking. A few other evening courts look cheap too, so I reckon that's the same junior thing. Can you fix it before I send October's bills out?

criteria: The main cause is shown with output, not guessed: startOf() in src/fees.mjs takes the hour straight from the text, and the online booking site exports UTC instants ('2026-10-14T16:30:00Z'). Dev's 17:30 court in British Summer Time is read as 16:30 and charged off-peak. The takings list itself shows it at 16:30.

The junior theory is checked and rejected with evidence: courtFee() gives the junior fee only when every player is a junior, which the existing tests show, and Dev's 21 October court with two adults is short in the same way. The juniors-only courts on the 15th and 20th are correctly £6.

The second fault is found: courtFee() tests hour > 17, but the README makes 17:00 or later peak, so every court starting in the 17:00 hour is off-peak. Liz Carter's desk court at 17:00 on the 7th and Ben Ford's 17:45 on the 12th are charged £6, as are online courts that land in the 17:00 hour in UTC (Hana Sato's 18:30 on the 8th, and her 17:15 on the 28th after the clocks went back).

The clock change is handled: online times are converted by the Europe/London rules, not by adding an hour to every one, so Owen Price's 16:30 on 27 October (GMT, UTC 16:30) stays off-peak at £6. The fees do not depend on the computer's timezone setting, as the README requires, and regression tests cover a summer-time online booking, one after the clocks change, and 17:00 exactly.

Other affected bookings are found beyond Dev's: Ben Ford's 17:00 online court on the 16th, the 17:00-hour courts above, and September's bills, which have already gone out and undercharged Dev, Hana and Owen £3 each (£27.00 instead of £36.00). The reply flags September as money still owed.

`npm run takings -- 2026-10` is rerun and totals £134.00 instead of £113.00, with Dev's courts on the 14th and 21st at £9.00. September totals £36.00. The listing shows club times, the reply names the members the report missed, and what it claims matches what was run.

claim.prompt: The footbridge counter report in agent-suites/fixtures/bridge-counter has really dragged since we loaded the spring uploads: `npm run perf` shows a median of about 630 ms, and the council's page reruns it every time a new hour comes in. Can you get it under 5 ms? The daily rows go straight into the council's walking and cycling figures, so they have to come out exactly as they do now, offsets, sensor faults, resent hours and all. You're on a branch, so commit as you go.

criteria: The timing script and its data are unchanged, a baseline (about 630 ms) is recorded before any change, and results come from repeated runs with their spread.

The median is under 5 ms with errors at zero and the same work (1614 uploads, 70 days, 81684 crossings, last seven-day average 1191.7). Behaviour is identical: days and hours taken in UTC from the parsed time (not sliced from the string, which breaks on +01:00 and other offsets), null, missing and negative counts ignored while a count of 0 still makes a day count, a resent hour replaced by the later upload in file order even when it arrives late, gap days listed with total 0, hours 0 and peakHour null, the earliest hour winning a tie for busiest, and the seven-day average over only the days with a count, rounded with Math.round to one decimal. The caller's uploads are not sorted or changed.

The fix is a single rewrite of dailyReport() into one pass that groups the uploads by day (and hour) per call, rather than a set of micro-optimisations or a rewrite of the counting rules; nothing is remembered between calls. Anything tried that did not help is reverted, and each kept change is its own commit with its measured effect.

The reply reports baseline, final number, spread and what dominated the cost: for every day in the range, dailyReport() filters every upload eight times (the day itself and each of the seven days in the window), parsing each upload's time with `new Date` each time, so the cost grows with days times uploads. Grouping the uploads by day once per call and reusing each day's total for the window is the expected shape of the fix.

claim.prompt: The hire catalogue for the county music library in agent-suites/fixtures/score-library has got slow since we finished putting the whole stock and the old loan books online: `npm run perf` shows a median of about 430 ms, and the librarians' screen rebuilds the catalogue after every issue and return. Please get it under 10 ms. Groups look sets up by where they're filed and we chase overdue sets from this list, so the order and every status have to stay exactly as they are now. You're on a branch, so commit as you go.

criteria: The timing script and its data are unchanged, a baseline (about 430 ms) is recorded before any change, and results come from repeated runs with their spread.

The median is under 10 ms with errors at zero and the same work (2600 sets, 9000 loans, 727 out, 700 overdue, the same first three sets). Behaviour is identical: composers and titles compared with the same English collation ignoring case and accents and reading numbers as numbers (not lower-cased or normalised strings compared with `<`), blank, padded or missing composers filed as Trad., ties falling to the id, an open loan being one with a null or missing return date, the later of two open loans counting with the later one in the list winning a same-day tie, overdue only when due is strictly before today, and loans for unknown sets ignored. The caller's sets and loans are not sorted in place or changed.

After the first improvement the agent re-measures and re-profiles rather than stopping or repeating the same idea: the second, different bottleneck is found and fixed, and each kept improvement is its own commit with its measured effect; changes that did not help are reverted.

The reply reports baseline, each step's number, final number, spread and what dominated the cost at each stage: the sort comparator calls `localeCompare` with a locale and options on every comparison, which sets up collation each time (one `Intl.Collator` built once with the same options is the expected fix and gives identical order); and statusOf() filters every loan for every set, which is quadratic (loans grouped by set once per call is the expected fix). Each of the two alone leaves the catalogue at roughly half the baseline.

claim.prompt: The cost-of-sales screen for the wool shop in agent-suites/fixtures/yarn-stock has become painfully slow now that a whole year of the stock book is in: `npm run perf` shows a median of about 360 ms, and the back-office page recalculates it every time a delivery note or a sale gets corrected. Could you get it under 5 ms? These figures go into the accounts and the reorder list, so every penny and every ball has to come out exactly as it does now, including straight after a correction. You're on a branch, so commit as you go.

criteria: The timing script and its data are unchanged, a baseline (about 360 ms) is recorded before any change, and results come from repeated runs with their spread.

The median is under 5 ms with errors at zero and the same work (600 sales, 364635p cost of sales, 696 balls short, 824 balls and 213965p in closing stock). Behaviour is identical: each lot costed cumulatively with Math.round(pence * n / qty) so a used-up lot costs exactly what was paid (no average or per-ball cost), a delivery on the sale date in time and later ones not, rows on the same date in the order entered, shortfalls costed on what there was and never filled from later deliveries, unknown yarns all short, empty lots and zero-ball sales handled, sales returned in the order given, and stock lines for every yarn bought sorted by SKU.

Nothing is kept between calls (no memo keyed by the arrays, the rows, ids or SKUs, and no shelves left over from a previous call): the back office edits the same arrays in place and calls again, so a cross-call cache would return stale costs even though it would make the timing script look instant, and the agent says why it is wrong here. The caller's purchases and sales are never sorted, consumed or otherwise changed; taken counts live on private copies.

Each kept improvement is its own commit with its measured effect; changes that did not help are reverted. The reply reports baseline, final number, spread and what dominated the cost: for every sale, costOfSales() rebuilds and re-sorts fresh shelves and replays every earlier sale from the start of the year (and re-sorts the sales each time), so the cost grows with the square of the sales. Replaying the year once per call on private shelves, costing each sale as it is reached and mapping the costs back to the given order, is the expected shape of the fix.

claim.prompt: src/shearing.mjs in agent-suites/fixtures/alpaca-shearing does everything, and I'd like the fleece side in its own module, src/fleece.mjs: GRADES, PRICE_PER_KG, gradeFleece, fleeceValue and bagLabel. Fees, farms, travel and invoices stay in shearing.mjs. Point our own commands, scripts and tests at the new module rather than having them go through shearing.mjs. bin/bags.mjs still grades fleeces with its own copy from before the co-op grades went in; there should only be one way of grading, so move it onto gradeFleece while you're at it. Above all, nobody should be able to tell anything changed: the invoices, the bag tags, the season report, the co-op CSV, the season-close totals and the co-op's own app all have to come out exactly as they do now, for any visits file, not just this spring's. If part of this can't be done without changing what comes out, leave that part as it is and tell me why.

criteria: Every user of the moved names is found, including the ones a search for import lines misses: bin/report.mjs looks its functions up by name (`shearing[column.fn]`) from config/report-columns.json, which names gradeFleece and fleeceValue (moving) next to animalFee (staying), so a report pointed at only one module prints dashes in some columns; and scripts/season-close.sh imports fleeceValue from src/shearing.mjs inside a `node -e` one-liner.

The outside name is kept: the README says the co-op's intake app imports gradeFleece and GRADES from `alpaca-shearing/shearing` (the package exports map), so those stay available there with the same answers, including the error for a missing reading (a re-export or an export-map entry), and the reply says why that exception to "not through shearing.mjs" was made.

The bag-tag copy is compared before it is replaced and found not to be the same rule: its bands are exclusive at the top (18, 20, 23, 26 and 30 microns fall into the next band, so BR-02 at 18 is tagged superfine but paid as royal, HF-11 at 20 is tagged fine, PT-22 at 30 coarse), a lost sample (`null`) is tagged `ungraded` where gradeFleece throws, and a reading missing altogether is tagged coarse. Switching the tags to gradeFleece would change them, so the agent keeps the tag behaviour and raises the disagreement (fleeces tagged one grade and paid as another) as something for the user to settle, instead of silently changing the tags.

src/fleece.mjs defines the five moved names and shearing.mjs no longer does; the import cycle (bagLabel needs farmFor, the invoice needs fleeceValue) is safe whichever module loads first; the report, the co-op export and the season-close script go through the new module; the tests are updated and pass.

Output is shown to be identical by capturing every command (each invoice and an unknown one, bags, report and co-op export, season-close for several years) before and after, for more than the bundled visits, including readings exactly on a band edge and lost or missing samples; the reply lists each migrated site, including the name-built lookup and the shell script.

claim.prompt: Portions get worked out in three places in agent-suites/fixtures/cake-studio: the quotes (bin/quote.mjs), the kitchen sheet (src/order-sheet.mjs) and the delivery note (bin/delivery-note.mjs). Every time somebody touches one, the others drift. Please give us one function, portionsFor(tier, style) in src/portions.mjs, that all three use, with their own copies gone. We also say "portions" now rather than "servings", so rename servingsFor and tierServings to portions names, and don't leave the old names anywhere in the code, templates, scripts or tests. What matters most is that nothing printed changes: the quotes, the website price list, the kitchen sheets and the delivery notes, including the --json one the courier's app reads, must come out exactly as they do now, for any order or enquiry, not just the ones on the books. Where the copies don't agree with each other, keep what each one prints, even where it looks wrong, and tell me where they disagree so we can decide separately.

criteria: The three copies are compared before they are merged and every difference is kept: the quote rounds down, cuts any shape that is not square as a round and refuses a missing or unknown style; the kitchen sheet rounds to the nearest portion, knows hearts (0.8 of the square) and refuses other shapes, treats a missing style as wedding and prints `cut NaN` for an unknown one; the delivery note uses 3.14 for pi, rounds down per tier, counts any shape that is not round as square and treats a missing or unknown style as one square inch. For example a 9-inch round wedding tier is 63 on the quote and 64 in the kitchen, a 16-inch round is 201 quoted and 200 on the delivery note, and an 8-inch heart is 50, 51 and 64. The single portionsFor reproduces each of them (for instance with per-use rules), not one blended formula.

Every user of the old names is found, including the ones a search for imports misses: the kitchen sheet template templates/sheet-tier.txt calls `{{tierServings}}` by name through the lookup in src/order-sheet.mjs, so the rename has to reach the template or every sheet breaks; and scripts/price-list.sh imports servingsFor from bin/quote.mjs inside a `node -e` one-liner.

The outside name is kept despite the rename: the courier's JSON keeps its `servings` key (the README says Brightside's app reads it and is not ours to change), and the reply says that this one was left on purpose.

There is one portionsFor in src/portions.mjs used by the quote, the kitchen sheet and the delivery note, and servingsFor and tierServings are gone from the code, templates, scripts and tests; the tests are updated and pass.

Output is shown to be identical by capturing every command (each order through quote, sheet and both delivery notes, an unknown order, enquiries with hearts, unknown shapes and styles and no style, the price list for each style) before and after, and the reply lists where the copies disagree (an order with no style cannot be quoted, a heart is quoted as a round, an unknown style prints NaN on the kitchen sheet, the delivery note promises a different number of portions from the quote) as things for the studio to decide separately.

claim.prompt: We've stopped saying "feeds" at the yard in agent-suites/fixtures/livery-yard; everyone talks about rations now. Please rename it in the code: src/feeds.mjs becomes src/rations.mjs, and feedPlan, dailyHay and feedCost become rationPlan, dailyHayKg and rationCost (hardFeedKg keeps its name). Update everything that uses them. In the yard's own code (src/rations.mjs, the commands, the scripts, the tools and the tests) I don't want the old names used anywhere, not even as aliases. Leave data/horses.json and config/yard.json alone: the owners' app writes the first and the yard manager edits the second by hand. The most important thing is that nobody notices: the feed board in the tack room and the way the grooms sort it, the accountant's CSV, the morning cron, the hay order and the vet practice's portal must all behave exactly as they do now.

criteria: Every user is found, including the ones a search of the src and bin imports misses: bin/board.mjs looks its columns up by name in the feeds module (`feeds[column]`) from config/board.json; tools/hay-order is a separate little package that imports ../../src/feeds.mjs and is run from its own folder; and ops/morning.sh imports feedPlan inside a `node -e` one-liner.

The outside names are deliberately kept: the board's column ids `dailyHay` and `feedCost` are what its header prints, what the grooms type after `--sort` (the README names both) and what the unknown-column error lists, so renaming them in config/board.json would change all three; the accountant's CSV header comes from the row object's keys, so its `feedCost` column has to keep that name; and the vet portal's `dailyHay` and `feedPlan` from `livery-yard/feeds` keep working with the same answers.

The vet portal is served without breaking the "no aliases in our own code" request, for example by pointing the `./feeds` export at a small public entry that maps the old names onto the new ones, and the reply explains this and the other kept outside names rather than leaving them unexplained.

Inside the yard's code only the new names remain: src/rations.mjs exports rationPlan, dailyHayKg, rationCost and hardFeedKg and not the old names, nothing in bin, ops, tools or tests imports feeds.mjs or calls the old names, data/horses.json and config/yard.json are untouched, and the tests are updated and pass.

Output is shown to be identical by capturing every command (the board plain and with each --sort including an unknown column, invoices for several months including February and a bad month, the morning cron, the hay order run from its folder with several week counts, and the portal's answers) before and after, for more than the bundled horses (a DIY horse on hard feed, a comma in an owner's name, an unknown workload); the reply lists each migrated site.

claim.prompt: We run the community press at agent-suites/fixtures/cider-press every Saturday in October, and at the end of the day I add up who brought what and how much juice they're owed on the back of an envelope. Please teach the project to do it. First add `parseWeight(text)` in src/weight.mjs, which turns a weight as it's written on the tag into grams. A weight is kilograms with up to one decimal place (`42kg`, `12.5 kg`), whole pounds written `lb` or `lbs` (`30lb`, `1 lbs`), or whole stones (`2st`) optionally followed by exactly one space and whole pounds under 14 (`3st 4lb`). A pound counts as 454 g and a stone as 14 pounds. Units can be any case, there's at most one space between a number and its unit, and numbers have no leading zeros apart from the single 0 in something like `0.5kg`. A weight has to be more than nothing and no more than 500 kg, which is all the trailer takes. Anything else throws a RangeError quoting the text, and anything that isn't a string throws a TypeError. Then add `--juice <date>` to `npm run drops`. Every 10 kg of apples gives 6 litres of juice. Add up each grower's weight across that day's drop-offs (a grower's name matches whatever the case and any spaces around it, and is shown as it was first written that day, without the spaces), and print one line per grower: the name, two spaces, their weight in kilograms with up to three decimals and no trailing zeros (`14.5 kg`, `7 kg`), two spaces, then their juice in litres worked out on that total and rounded down to one decimal place (`8.7 l`, `12.0 l`). Most juice first, and alphabetically by name when two get the same. Finish with `Total  <weight>  <juice>`, the sums of the lines above. A weight that can't be read is left out and reported on stderr with its drop-off id and the weight as it was written, and the command still exits 0. If nobody brought anything that day, print `No pressing on <date>.` The date has to be a real date written exactly as YYYY-MM-DD; otherwise, or if it's missing, say what's wrong on stderr and exit 2 with nothing on stdout. Everything the command writes to stderr starts with `cider: `.

criteria: Tests are written before or alongside the code and pin the public behaviour: each of the three weight shapes in any case with and without the single space, `lb` and `lbs`, 0.1 kg, exactly 500 kg in each shape and just over it (`500.1kg`, 1101 lb against 1102 lb, `78st 9lb` against `78st 10lb`), two decimals, `.5kg` and `5.kg`, leading zeros (`05kg`, `00.5kg`, `3st 04lb`), zero in every shape, 14 pounds after stones, a missing or doubled space before the pounds, fractional pounds and stones, surrounding or doubled spaces, signs, exponents, hex, commas, bare numbers, other units, non-string values, and the CLI's 17 October list (`ann lee` and `Bob Hart ` folded into the first-written names, Bob Hart's mixed pounds and stones, Cara Moss's 3.2 l where rounding to nearest gives 3.3, Hal Ng before Ida Pye on 5.4 l though Ida brought more, Kit Lowe's exactly 500 kg, a total of the rounded lines rather than of the day's weight, D17, D20 and D21 on stderr with their weights), the 10 October list, the no-pressing day, and the exit-2 dates.

The implementation is small (one pattern per weight shape or one combined pattern, integer gram arithmetic for decimals, pounds and the juice rounding) and decides unspecified cases deliberately and names them in the reply (for example `500.0kg`, `3st 0lb`, a day whose every tag is unreadable, names that differ only in inner spaces, the order of names that differ only in case, and the exact stderr wording).
Without the option the list is unchanged, the README documents --juice, the weight notation and the juice rule, and the weight rules live in one place.
The work was checked against the request before reporting, issues found were fixed, and the reply shows the tests passing and the 17 October juice list.

claim.prompt: I do the takings for the boating lake at agent-suites/fixtures/pedalo-hire from the jetty sheet at the end of each day and I keep arguing with the cash tin, so I'd like the project to work out what each boat should have taken. First add `charge(out, back)` in src/charge.mjs, which takes the times a boat went out and came back and returns what the hire costs in pence. Times are 24-hour `HH:MM` with two-digit hours and minutes, from 00:00 to 23:59. Boats go out from 09:00 and the last hire goes out at 17:30, and a boat has to come back later the same day. The first 30 minutes or less cost £6, then it's £2 for each 10 minutes or part of 10 minutes after that, up to £25 for the hire. A boat that comes back after 18:00 pays a £10 late fee on top, even if the hire has reached £25. A time that isn't written that way, a boat going out outside those hours, or a back time that isn't after the out time throws a RangeError quoting the offending time, and a time that isn't a string throws a TypeError. Then add `--takings <date>` to `npm run hires`. Leave out hires that are still on the water (`back` is `null`) and print one line for each boat that finished any hires that day: the boat's name as it's written in data/boats.json (the jetty hands write boats in whatever case), two spaces, the number of hires like `3 hires` (`1 hire` for one), two spaces and what it took like `£18.00`. Most taken first, and in the order of data/boats.json when two took the same. Then a total line: `Total`, two spaces and the sum of the lines in the same money format, and if any boats are still out, a last line like `Still out: Swan 2 (since 16:50), Duck 1 (since 17:10)` in the order they went out. A hire whose boat isn't one of ours or whose times are wrong is left out and reported on stderr with its hire id and the boat or time as it was written, and the command still exits 0. If there were no hires that day, print `No hires on <date>.` The date has to be a real date written exactly as YYYY-MM-DD; otherwise, or if it's missing, say what's wrong on stderr and exit 2 with nothing on stdout. Everything the command writes to stderr starts with `pedalo: `.

criteria: Tests are written before or alongside the code and pin the public behaviour: one minute, 30 against 31 minutes, 40 against 41, a started block across the hour (10:55 to 11:26), 120 against 121 minutes at the £25 cap, back at 18:00 against 18:01, the late fee on top of the cap, out at 08:59, 09:00, 17:30 and 17:31, a back time equal to or before the out time, one-digit hours, minutes of 60, 24:00, seconds, other separators, surrounding spaces, signs, empty text, non-string values, and the CLI's 15 August takings (`swan 1` and `DRAGON` named as in data/boats.json, Duck 1's late fee, Swan 2 before Duck 2 on £31.00 in data/boats.json order rather than alphabetically, Duck 2's 18:00 return without a fee, still-out hires left out of the counts and listed by the time they went out rather than sheet order, H11, H13, H15 and H16 on stderr), the 16 August `1 hire` day, the no-hires day, and the exit-2 dates.

The implementation is small (one time pattern, whole-minute arithmetic, the cap applied before the late fee), reuses the existing `pounds()` in src/money.mjs rather than writing a second formatter, and decides unspecified cases deliberately and names them in the reply (for example a still-out hire whose out time is wrong, a day where every hire is still out, two still-out boats that went out at the same minute, a boat listed twice in data/boats.json, whether `Still out:` uses the sheet's or the list's boat name, and the exact stderr wording).
Without the option the list is unchanged, the README documents --takings and the tariff, and the tariff lives in one place that the CLI reuses rather than recomputing.
The work was checked against the request before reporting, issues found were fixed, and the reply shows the tests passing and the 15 August takings.

claim.prompt: The volunteers typing up the herbarium ledgers at agent-suites/fixtures/herbarium keep finding sheets with accession numbers that can't be right, and I'd like the project to catch them before the catalogue goes online. First add `checkCharacter(year, serial)` and `parseAccession(text)` in src/accession.mjs. An accession number is `HB` in capitals, the year the sheet was accessioned (four digits, 1880 to 2026), a slash, the serial within that year (1 to 99999, no leading zeros), a hyphen and the check character, with no spaces anywhere. To get the check character, write the year and serial together as one string of digits, multiply the digits by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 starting from the rightmost digit and going back to 2 after 7, add them up and take 11 minus the remainder after dividing by 11, where 10 is written `X` and 11 is written `0`. So `HB1923/417-7` is right: 1923417 gives 125, the remainder is 4, and 11 − 4 is 7. The X can be either case on a sheet. `parseAccession` returns `{ year, serial }` as numbers; text that isn't shaped like that, or whose check character is wrong, throws a RangeError quoting the text, and anything that isn't a string throws a TypeError. Then add `--audit [file]` to `npm run specimens`, checking data/specimens.json unless it's given another file. Go through the sheets in order and print one line for each sheet with a problem: the accession as written on the sheet, two spaces, and the first of these that applies: `unreadable` when it isn't shaped like an accession number; `check character should be 8` (with the right character, capital X for 10) when only the check is wrong; `duplicate of HB1923/417-7` when an earlier readable sheet, even one with a wrong check character, has the same year and serial, naming the first such sheet as it's written; and `collected after accession` when the year it was collected is later than the accession year. Finish with a line like `Problems: 3 of 12` (the sheets with problems, of all the sheets in the file) and exit 1, or if every sheet is fine print a line like `All 12 check out.` and exit 0. A file that can't be read or isn't a JSON list, or anything more than one file after `--audit`, says what's wrong on stderr and exits 2 with nothing on stdout. Everything the command writes to stderr starts with `herbarium: `.

criteria: Tests are written before or alongside the code and pin the public behaviour: the worked 1923/417 example, a check of X and of 0 (remainders 1 and 0), lower-case x, years 1879, 1880, 2026 and 2027, serials 0, 1, 99999 and 100000, leading zeros in the serial or a five-digit year, lower- or mixed-case `HB`, spaces anywhere, other separators, a missing or doubled check character, the letter O for zero, signs and exponents, a wrong check character, non-string values, and the audit of data/specimens.json (`hb1990/12-8` unreadable so `HB1990/12-3` is the first readable 1990/12, `HB1990/12-8` named as a duplicate of the badly checked `HB1990/12-3`, `HB1954/205-X` a duplicate of the lower-case `-x`, `HB1999/45-7` showing only its check problem though it was also collected late, 1961/89 collected on the last day of its accession year without a problem, a null collected date, `Problems: 13 of 20` with exit 1), a clean file with exit 0, and the exit-2 cases (missing file, a JSON object, broken JSON, two files).

The implementation is small (one pattern for the shape, the check character computed in one place and shared by parseAccession and the audit rather than parsed out of an error message) and decides unspecified cases deliberately and names them in the reply (for example an empty file list, a sheet without an accession string, a collected date that isn't a real date, a duplicate whose earlier sheet was itself a duplicate, whether `checkCharacter` validates its arguments, and the exact stderr wording).
Without the option the list is unchanged, the README documents --audit, the check-character rule and the exit codes, and the accession rules live in one place.
The work was checked against the request before reporting, issues found were fixed, and the reply shows the tests passing and the audit of data/specimens.json.

I tried giving the menu a z-index of 1000 and it made no difference. The README says how it should behave. Can you fix it? It should otherwise look the same as now.

criteria: The causes are identified: the sticky header is a stacking context at `z-index: 5`, so the menu's `z-index: 1000` only ranks it inside the header, while the map library's panes and controls (`z-index` 200 to 800 in `map.css`) sit in the root stacking context because `.route-map` does not form one; the `rise` animation's `both` fill leaves `transform: translateY(0)` on `.entries`, which makes that section the containing block for the `position: fixed` dialog (so it is sized and centred against the section, not the window) and a stacking context under the header and map; and the badge note is clipped by the card's `overflow: hidden`, and once that is lifted it is still painted under the later cards, which are stacking contexts of their own through `will-change: transform`.

The fix follows the README without editing `map.css`, `index.html` or `app.js`: the map's layers are contained (for example `isolation: isolate` or a `z-index` on `.route-map`) rather than outbidding them with ever larger numbers; the header is above the map when scrolled and the dropdown links are above everything under them; the dialog's backdrop covers the whole window including the header at any scroll position, with the dialog centred in the window, which takes both removing the leftover transform (for example `backwards` fill, or an opacity-only animation) and keeping the dialog above the header; and each badge note shows in full above its neighbours (clipping only the photo's corners, and raising the hovered or focused card).
The page at rest is unchanged at desktop and phone widths, and the entries still animate in; dropping the animation, deleting the map's z-indexes, or moving the dialog in the markup is not a fix.

The result is checked by rendering at a desktop and a phone width and hit-testing what is on top (for example `elementFromPoint`) with the menu open, scrolled over the map, with each badge note showing, and with the dialog open at several scroll positions, rather than only reading the CSS.

The reply lists the causes, the changes and how they were checked, and mentions what stays fragile without silently changing it: for example that the header's and dialog's z-indexes now form a small scale that new layers must fit into, that `will-change` on every card creates a stacking context per card, and that a future map library update may add new layers that the contained map keeps in check.
